reason: The sources provide over 15 cross-supported claims from multiple distinct sites covering Venus's retrograde spin, day length, atmospheric pressure, and super-rotation.
story: Venus is one of the most bizarre worlds in our solar system. Unlike almost every other planet, Venus spins backward in a retrograde clockwise direction. If you could stand on its scorched surface, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east. Even stranger, a single rotation takes about 243 Earth days—meaning a day on Venus is actually longer than its 224.7-day orbital year! But while the planet's solid body barely turns, its toxic atmosphere of 96.5% carbon dioxide super-rotates, whipping around the world in just four Earth days. Under a crushing surface pressure 92 times that of Earth and temperatures reaching 464 °C, Venus presented a bizarre mystery to early space probes like Pioneer Venus and Venus Express. From mysterious dark cloud absorbers affecting its weather to controversial hints of atmospheric phosphine, Venus continues to defy planetary norms.
angle: On Venus, a single day lasts longer than an entire year, and the Sun rises in the west because the planet spins backward.

claims.claim: Venus rotates in a retrograde, clockwise direction, opposite to most other planets.
Because of its backward spin, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east on Venus.
Venus takes about 243 Earth days to complete one single rotation on its axis.
Venus completes an orbit around the Sun once every 224 to 224.7 Earth days.
A single rotation of Venus on its axis takes longer than its entire orbital year around the Sun.
Venus's atmosphere super-rotates, circling the entire planet in just four Earth days.
The surface atmosphere of Venus reaches average temperatures of 737 K to 740 K (464 °C to 467 °C).
The surface atmospheric pressure on Venus is 92 to 93 bars, about 92 times greater than Earth's sea-level pressure.
Venus's atmosphere is composed of 96.5% carbon dioxide and 3.5% nitrogen.
Near the surface of Venus, wind speeds are slow, averaging between 0.3 and 1.0 meters per second.
The atmospheric density at the surface of Venus is approximately 65 kg/m³.
Sulfur dioxide concentrations in Venus's upper atmosphere dropped by a factor of 10 after initial recorded spikes.
Dark patches called unknown absorbers in Venus's clouds absorb solar radiation and directly influence the planet's weather.
Carl Sagan proposed the hypothesis that microorganisms could live in Venus's upper atmosphere.
Phosphine gas was reported in Venus's atmosphere using spectral detections from the JCMT and ALMA radio telescopes.
Phosphine is considered a potential biomarker gas because its presence could indicate biological activity.

disputed: Mechanism of Venusian spin reversal: Scientific American notes scientists dispute whether Venus flipped its axis 180 degrees due to solar tidal forces or slowed to a stop and reversed direction (attribute: 'according to theoretical models').

Detection and concentration of phosphine gas: Sources dispute the exact abundance of phosphine, with initial reports claiming ~20 ppb while re-analyses found data processing errors lowering it to 1 ppb or zero (attribute: 'according to initial telescopic observations, which remain contested').

Origin of upper atmosphere sulfur dioxide spikes: ESA and Wikipedia sources disagree on whether spikes are caused by active volcanic eruptions or atmospheric circulation cycles (attribute: 'researchers attribute the changes to either active volcanism or atmospheric circulation').

Presence of atmospheric lightning: Wikipedia sources note VLF and whistler mode detections suggesting lightning, while Akatsuki and Parker Solar Probe data show low or non-planetary signals (attribute: 'planetary scientists continue to debate whether lightning occurs').
